lead: An optical network is a set of nodes joined by fiber links. A connection that stays in the optical domain from one end to the other is a lightpath, and it holds one wavelength on every link it crosses. Networks exist because one fiber between two points is not enough: many users, many cities and many services must share the same fiber plant. Telephone companies use these ideas in access, metro and core networks; the same words describe a campus fiber ring or a data-centre link.
prereq: You need: WDM channels on one fiber (WDM concepts) and the point-to-point link and its power budget (see Link power budget).

blocks.text: A node is a point where traffic is added, dropped, switched or regenerated. A link is the fiber between two adjacent nodes. In an amplified link, a span is the fiber between two amplifiers, so one long link can hold several spans; some books use span and link for the same thing on short unamplified routes. A path is the ordered list of nodes and links from a source to a destination. A channel is one wavelength on one link.

A lightpath is an end-to-end connection that uses one wavelength on every link of its path and is not converted to electronics in between; some books call it a wavelength path. The physical topology is the actual graph of nodes and fibers. The logical (lightpath) topology is the graph of lightpaths that the routers see. A ring of fibers can carry a full mesh of lightpaths, as the worked example shows.

A transparent network keeps the signal optical end to end; impairments add up along the path (see Signal degradation in optical fibers), so the reach is limited. An opaque network regenerates at nodes: it receives, reamplifies, reshapes and retimes the signal, then retransmits it (3R). Regeneration restores the signal but costs a transponder pair at each node.

Common physical topologies are mesh, ring, star and bus. A mesh has many links and survives cuts but needs more ports. A ring is a closed loop; two fibers in opposite directions form a self-healing ring. A star has one central node, and a bus shares one fiber.

The public telecommunication network has three tiers. The access network joins homes, offices and mobile towers to the first exchange, over a few kilometres up to about 20 km; a passive optical network splits one fiber among many users. The metro network joins the exchanges of a city over tens of kilometres, usually as a ring, because ducts follow the roads and a ring gives a second route. The core (long-haul) network joins cities and countries over hundreds to thousands of kilometres as a mesh of cross-connects and amplifiers; a Delhi–Mumbai route is a core link. Access fights cost per user, metro fights fast protection, and core fights capacity and reach.

Traffic crosses these networks in two transmission modes. In circuit switching a fixed path and capacity are set up before any data flows and held until the call ends: a SONET/SDH time slot (SONET/SDH) or a whole lightpath. In packet switching the data is cut into packets that share the links on demand, each carrying an address (IP) or a short connection label (an ATM virtual circuit, Network layers and ATM). Circuits give fixed delay; packets use spare capacity better.

An optical node does four jobs. Add/drop puts local wavelengths into or out of the fiber (an optical add-drop multiplexer, OADM). Cross-connect moves a wavelength from an input fiber to a chosen output fiber (an optical cross-connect, OXC). Regeneration recreates a clean signal when the path is too long. Switching sets or changes routes under control. The node hardware is in WDM networks, optical nodes and switching.

Protection reserves capacity before a failure. In 1+1 the signal is sent on two paths at once and the receiver selects the better copy; the backup carries no other traffic. In 1:1 one backup path stands by for one working path and may carry low-priority extra traffic while the working path is healthy. In 1:N one backup serves N working paths. Restoration finds a new route only after the failure, so it is slower and needs a control plane. Metro networks favour rings because a cut is handled by switching at the two nodes next to it, within milliseconds.

A broadcast-and-select network sends every wavelength to every node, and each receiver filters the one it wants. A wavelength-routed network sends each wavelength through cross-connects along its own path, so the same wavelength can be reused on links that do not overlap. Static lightpaths are set up once; switched lightpaths are set up and torn down by signalling.

examples.question: A metro ring has 6 nodes, A to F. Every pair of nodes needs one bidirectional 10 Gb/s lightpath, which uses the same wavelength on both fibers of each link it crosses. (a) How many lightpaths are there? (b) How many wavelengths are needed if no wavelength is reused? (c) How many with dedicated 1+1 protection on separate wavelengths, still with no reuse? (d) What working traffic is carried? (e) With shortest routes and reuse, what is the fewest wavelengths possible?
steps: (a) Count each pair once: N(N − 1)/2 = 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 lightpaths.
(b) With no reuse, each lightpath has its own wavelength on the whole ring: 15 wavelengths.
(c) Dedicated 1+1 sends a second copy on a separate wavelength over the other side of the ring: 2 × 15 = 30 wavelengths.
(d) Each lightpath carries 10 Gb/s in each direction: 15 × 10 = 150 Gb/s in each direction, 300 Gb/s counting both. The protection copies repeat the same data, so they add no working traffic.

(e) Shortest routes: the 6 neighbour pairs use 1 link each, the 6 pairs two apart use 2 links, and the 3 opposite pairs use 3 links. Link uses = 6 × 1 + 6 × 2 + 3 × 3 = 27 over 6 links, an average of 4.5, so the busiest link must carry at least 5 lightpaths and at least 5 wavelengths are needed.

Five are enough: route the opposite pairs A–D via B, B–E via A, C–F via D, and colour the lightpaths so that no two sharing a link get the same wavelength. One such set is λ1 = {A–D, A–E, D–E}, λ2 = {B–D, B–E}, λ3 = {A–C, A–F, C–F}, λ4 = {B–C, B–F, C–E, E–F}, λ5 = {A–B, C–D, D–F}.
Check: links A–B, C–D and E–F each carry 5 lightpaths and the other three links carry 4, so 4 × 3 + 5 × 3 = 27 link uses, as counted.
examples.answer: 15 lightpaths; 15 wavelengths without reuse; 30 with dedicated 1+1; 150 Gb/s of working traffic in each direction (300 Gb/s both ways); with reuse on shortest routes, 5 wavelengths.

traps: Physical topology is not the lightpath topology. A ring of fiber can carry a full mesh of lightpaths, so do not copy the fiber graph into the logical graph.
Count a bidirectional lightpath once per pair, N(N − 1)/2, and give its traffic per direction. Counting each node’s demands separately gives 30 demands and doubles the traffic.
Dedicated 1+1 on separate wavelengths doubles the wavelengths used; 1:N shares one backup among N working paths and does not.
A lightpath needs the same wavelength on every link unless a converter is present. A free wavelength on one link is not enough.
1+1 and 1:1 both have a backup, but in 1+1 the signal is always sent on both paths; only a 1:1 backup can carry extra traffic while healthy.

quiz.q: Define a lightpath and a channel.
quiz.a: A lightpath is an end-to-end optical connection that uses one wavelength on every link of its path. A channel is one wavelength on one link.

quiz.q: Name the three tiers of the public telecommunication network.
Why can the logical topology differ from the physical topology?
quiz.a: The physical topology is the graph of fibers and nodes; the logical topology is the graph of lightpaths set up over them. One fiber ring can carry a full mesh of lightpaths, as the 6-node ring with 15 lightpaths shows.

quiz.q: Contrast a transparent network with an opaque network.
quiz.a: A transparent network keeps the signal optical end to end, so impairments add up and the reach is limited. An opaque network regenerates at nodes with 3R, which restores the signal but costs transponders at each node.

quiz.q: A 5-node ring gives one bidirectional 10 Gb/s lightpath to each pair, with no wavelength reuse and dedicated 1+1 protection. Find (a) the number of lightpaths, (b) the wavelengths, (c) the working traffic.
quiz.a: (a) 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 lightpaths. (b) 10 working wavelengths; 1+1 on separate wavelengths doubles this to 20. (c) 10 × 10 = 100 Gb/s in each direction.

quiz.q: On the 5-node ring with shortest routes, what is the least number of wavelengths if they can be reused?
quiz.a: The 5 neighbour pairs use 1 link and the 5 pairs two apart use 2 links: 5 + 10 = 15 link uses over 5 links, exactly 3 per link. So at least 3 wavelengths are needed, and a careful colouring shows 3 are enough, against 10 without reuse.

quiz.q: Why do metro networks use rings more than meshes?
quiz.a: City ducts follow the roads and close into loops, so a ring matches the plant. A ring gives two separate routes between any two nodes, so a single cut is handled by switching at the two nodes next to it, fast and simply, with fewer ports than a mesh.

In 1+1 the signal is sent on both paths all the time and the receiver selects one, so switching is fastest but the backup carries nothing else. In 1:1 the backup is reserved for one working path and may carry low-priority traffic while the working path is healthy; that traffic is dropped when protection is needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real metro and core networks now use reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexers and colourless, directionless cross-connects, so a lightpath can be changed without touching fiber. Software-defined control sets up switched lightpaths automatically, and elastic optical networks give each channel only the spectrum it needs. Search next for ROADM, flexible grid and optical network control plane.

Right: the same nodes as the routers see them, a full mesh of 15 lightpaths, coloured by the five wavelengths that are enough when wavelengths are reused.
